books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

primary_sources: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity” (1839)

stimulus.text: John L. O’Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, November 1839: “American patriotism is not of soil; we are not aborigines, nor of ancestry, for we are of all nations; but it is essentially personal enfranchisement, for ‘where liberty dwells,’ said Franklin, the sage of the Revolution, ‘there is my country.’” O’Sullivan also wrote that “the nation of many nations is destined to manifest to mankind the excellence of divine principles.”
stimulus.source_note: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, vol. 6, no. 23 (November 1839), pp. 426-430. Verbatim quotations verified against Wikisource. Survivor rewrite of pr25e-test1-q18: new stimulus passage, new stem, new options, new explanations.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: When O'Sullivan calls America a “nation of many nations,” he most likely means that Americans

options.text: came from many different nations through immigration
conquered many nations in war overseas
options.misconception: O'Sullivan writes about peoples coming to America, not about America conquering other nations.

options.text: traded with many nations overseas for goods
options.misconception: The phrase is about the peoples who make up the nation, not about trade partners.
O'Sullivan's “many nations” are the nations immigrants came from; he writes “we are not aborigines.”

rationales.A: O'Sullivan opens by saying Americans “derived their origin from many other nations.” A nation of many nations is a nation built by immigrants from many places.
rationales.B: The essay celebrates peoples joining America, not armies conquering abroad. Conquest is not his subject here.
rationales.C: Trade partners are other nations, not the nation itself. O'Sullivan means the peoples inside America.
rationales.D: Native peoples are the ones he excludes with “we are not aborigines.” His many nations are the immigrants' home nations.
rationales.general:
1. Find his opening sentence. Americans derived their origin from many other nations.
2. Match the phrase to that sentence. Many nations means many origins.
3. Answer from the opening. The nation is made of immigrants.
Background: The two largest immigrant groups of the period came from Ireland and the German states, in northern and western Europe.
Remember: an author's opening sentence often holds the key to a phrase later in the piece.
